nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Subtropical sun powers the forest. Falls spray and clearings let different plants thrive.

nodes.name: Rain and river mist
nodes.desc: Wikipedia gives the Alto Parana forest roughly 1,200 to 1,600 mm of rain a year, with a drier season from April to September.

nodes.name: Iguazu River and falls
nodes.desc: The river runs about 23 km through the park past the falls. Spray and river moisture keep the riverbank forest dense and green.

nodes.name: Forest soil
nodes.desc: Leaf litter and fallen fruit build the soil that the forest trees draw on.

nodes.name: Ambay pumpwood
nodes.desc: A fast-growing pioneer tree of forest edges and clearings. It is among the best-recorded plants near the park and is eaten by tapirs and capuchins in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Queen palm
nodes.desc: Its sticky orange-pulped fruit is eaten by toucans, coatis, tapirs, agoutis and many birds, which spread the seeds.

nodes.name: Inga
nodes.desc: A legume tree of the Atlantic Forest whose fruit is eaten by tapirs, capuchins and birds in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Iguana hackberry
nodes.desc: A hackberry shrub or tree. Its fruit is widely eaten by forest mammals and birds in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Lowland tapir
nodes.desc: A browsing herbivore that eats leaves, shoots and fruit. Wikipedia says tapirs swallow many forest seeds and so help spread them.

nodes.name: Azara's agouti
nodes.desc: A forest rodent that eats palm fruit and seeds, and often buries them, which can start new palms.

nodes.name: Collared peccary
nodes.desc: A pig-like forest herb and fruit eater that travels in groups, and is prey for jaguars and pumas.

nodes.name: Red brocket
nodes.desc: A small forest deer that browses leaves and fallen fruit, and is a regular prey of jaguars and pumas.

nodes.name: Black capuchin
nodes.desc: An omnivorous monkey eating fruit, insects, eggs and small animals.

nodes.name: Toco toucan
nodes.desc: A big-billed fruit eater that spreads seeds, and also takes lizards and nestlings. Wikipedia lists it among the large toucans of Iguazu.

nodes.name: Butterflies
nodes.desc: Many butterflies live here, and the park is known for them. Caterpillars chew leaves, adults feed on fruit, sap or nectar.

nodes.name: South American coati
nodes.desc: An omnivore that climbs to eat fruit, hunts invertebrates and eggs, and is itself preyed on by jaguars.

nodes.name: Ocelot
nodes.desc: A small spotted cat that hunts agoutis, monkeys and other mid-sized forest animals. Wikipedia lists it as rare at Iguazu.

nodes.name: Argentine tegu
nodes.desc: A big omnivorous lizard eating insects, eggs, fruit and carrion. Cougars and jaguars are among its predators.

nodes.name: Black vulture
nodes.desc: A scavenger that mostly eats carrion and is very commonly recorded near the park.

nodes.name: Great dusky swift
nodes.desc: Catches insects in the air and nests on cliffs beside or behind waterfalls, flying through the spray of falls such as Iguazu.

nodes.name: Jaguar
nodes.desc: The top predator, taking prey from peccary and deer to capybara and caiman. Wikipedia lists it as threatened at Iguazu.

nodes.name: Puma
nodes.desc: A wide-ranging cat that takes mostly smaller prey than the jaguar, from agoutis to deer.

nodes.name: Fungi and leaf-litter decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, fruit and carcasses so nutrients return to the forest soil.
